Shortly before 3 o'clock this afternoon, one of the most terrible tragedies in the history of Leadville took place on upper Harrison avenue, the victim being Officer Samuel Townsend, one of the oldest and most popular officers of Leadville, and his slayer, Thomas C. Early, a leading young lawyer of this place. At the hour mentioned, the passers-by on Harrison avenue, near the corner of Fifth, were startled at the loud report of three pistol shots, one following the other in quick succession, and a thin, blue cloud of smoke, that curled and drifted from the hallway of the Union block, located the spot where one man stood with heated weapon clenched within his hand and another writhed in the agonies of dissolution. The crowd that hurried around the hallway were horror-stricken to see the well-known form of Officer Sam Townsend, the constable of Judge Talbot's court, prone upon the landing. Mr. T. C. Early was standing on the stairs, a few steps above, and paused, irresolute which way to go. His hat lay at his feet, and his clothing was disheveled, as though from a recent struggle. Fortunately among the first who were at the spot was Captain John Byrne, the detective in the city's employ, and taking in the situation at a glance, he placed Early under arrest, and hurried with him into Babcock's hat store next door. 'Ere this time the word that a murder had been committed, passed with lightning-like rapidity from mouth to mouth, and the pavement was blocked by a dense crowd that surged into the street and well nigh trampled one upon the other in their effort to reach the scene of the killing. As Byrne arrested Early, several gentlemen lifted Townsend up and carried him across the street to Dr. Dodge's drug store, where he was laid upon a pallet placed upon the floor, and Drs. He was suffering the greatest agony, and it was only with the greatest difficulty that he could be held down while an examination of his injuries was made. His garments were pulled open, and in the abdomen, about three inches above the right groin, a ghastly wound was revealed. The leaden messenger of destruction had buried itself in his bowels, and it was well nigh certain that death was only a matter of the briefest time. A messenger had been sent at once to his wife, and, with his little boy, she arrived in a few moments. The poor woman was scarcely able to realize the magnitude of the blow that had fallen upon her, and kneeling with streaming and agonized eyes by her husband's side, she pressed his hand convulsively to her breast, while the little one with great bewildered eyes stood holding to her dress. It was a sight that will never leave the memory of those who witnessed it.

A FORMER SEDALIAN
Kills a Constable in Leadville and is Rescued With Difficulty From a Mob.
Thomas C. Early, who formerly resided here, and who left Sedalia for Leadville, Col., some three years ago, at which latter place he has since resided, shot and killed a constable there on Monday. j-c-early-leadville-1882-03-28.A12: Samuel C. Townsend of Leadville, Col., was brutally shot down in broad daylight, on the streets of that city, Tuesday, March 28. The trouble which led to the terrible deed grew out of a matter of costs in a justice court, Early claiming that Mr. Townsend had over charged him 10 or 15 cents. A dispute arose, and without warning Early drew a pistol from his pocket and fired at Townsend. Mr. Townsend endeavored to wrench the weapon from him. In the struggle the pistol was again discharged, the ball entering the abdomen of Mr. Townsend and lodging in the spine The wounded man lived only about half an hour. The murderer was soon under arrest. He claimed to have acted in self-defense only, but the testimony of two or three eye-witnesses, shows that Mr. Townsend did not strike the man nor attempt to shoot him, as Early claimed; and when he was picked up his pistol was found in his ulster with all its chambers loaded. Mr. Townsend was a native of Vermont. He was born in Wallingford in December, 1849; there he resided most of the time until 1871, when he went to Colorado and engaged in sheep-raising. In 1874 he was elected assessor and the year following sheriff of Rio Grande county, Colorado, afterwards serving as marshal of Del Norte and Alamrosa. In the latter town he married Miss Allie Allen, who, with one child, a boy, survives him.—Rutland Herald.

The Justice finally announced the examination over, and remanded the prisoners to the custody of the Sheriff for indictment and trial at the April term of the District Court. He had hardly uttered the words before strong men seized every officer in the room and tightly held them, and other men seized Sullivan and Howard, lifting them up as though they were small children, and started on a run for the place set for the execution. A THIRD VICTIM.

The double execution was no sooner over than about 400 members of the Committee of Safety marched to the County Jail and demanded the person of Benjamin Payne, there confined for the murder of police officer Siers in October last. The officer in charge refused to surrender him, when the committee proceeded to take him whether or no. They tore down the jail fence, and cut and beat down the three doors between them and the assassin. They soon had him in their hands, and two minutes later had him at the place of execution. A third rope had been thrown over the beam, and Payne was quickly drawn up between the other two men. The three were allowed to hang there half an hour or so longer, when all were removed to the untaker's rooms and shortly after buried.

MURDERERS LYNCHED.
A Committee of Safety at Seattle, W. T, Execute Three Murderers.
SEATTLE, W. T., Jan. 19.—James Sullivan and Wm. Howard were arrested here to-day on the charge of the murder of Geo. R. Reynolds, a young man whom they waylaid and shot last night. The evidence of their guilt is most conclusive. The feeling was intense, and at the close of the preliminary examination a committee of safety forced its way into the court room, and, overpowering the officers, took the prisoners, Sullivan and Howard, a short distance and hanged them. The bodies were left suspended, and the crowd, numbering over four hundred, then proceeded to the county jail, and overcoming the guards and breaking down the doors of the cell, took out Benjamin Payne, who was confined for the murder of police officer Sears. He was taken to the place were the bodies of Sullivan and Howard were suspended, and hung. The bodies were left hanging sometime, and then given over to the coroner. The committee of safety continue their organization, and have issued notice that persons guilty of highway robbery in the city will, if arrested, receive the penalty of death in a summary manner.

The three highway robberies and the formation of a vigilance committee in Seattle last week, resulted in a neck-tie party, as predicted. On Tuesday night the two robbers who murdered George B. Reynolds were found concealed in the hay on a wharf, within three hours after the murder. They were delivered over to the officers of the law, and on Wednesday were examined before a justice of the peace. The evidence produced proved beyond a doubt that these two persons, giving their names as James Sullivan and Wm. Howard, were the same who shot Reynolds and also attempted to rob Capt. Weeks and the Rev. J. C. Fair. The justice committed them to await the action of the grand jury, but the words were not fairly out of his mouth when the vigilance committee seized the officers and prisoners, the latter being carried out to Occident square, where a scaffold had been prepared, and in two minutes the men were strung up, in the presence of over 2000 of the people, at 1:30 P. Never since I have been in this Territory has the law allowed a juror to be excluded on the ground that he has formed or expressed an opinion, and never so far as I know has one been excluded on such a ground. Indictments in Washington Territory are in the highest degree untechnical, and are by express statute made sufficient and have by the Courts been repeatedly held sufficient, if the act or omission charged as crime is clearly and distinctly set forth in ordinary and concise language, in such a manner as to enable a person of common understanding to know what is intended. Postponement of a criminal trial is a rare thing in this Territory, and is never granted without good cause shown, while expensive and protracted criminal trials, such as we once in a while hear of elsewhere, through the the press, are so far as I know things that never have occurred. Witnesses sometimes have to be brought great distances, and the mileage and per diem we pay is high, so that costs sometimes mount up to a considerable sum, but that is due to the sparse settlement of our immense domain and to our disposition to compensate well those whom we compel to attend our Courts.

By the records of this district it appears, that during the last twelve years—and I cannot go back further because the records are imperfect—there have been thirty persons arrested and indicted for homicide under the Territorial law; of these none that I know of escaped before trial except one temporarily, and only one was discharged without trial. Twenty-nine out of the thirty were tried. The trials of twenty-one came off within eight days after indictment. Two of the twenty-nine trials occupied four days, one three days and none of the rest to exceed two days. Only six continuances for one term were granted and three for two terms; one of the former because the jury disagreed; one because the prisoner was a woman great with child and could not be tried without endangering the life of her child as well as her own; one of the latter because at the first term the prisoner could not get his witnesses and at the second had escaped into British Columbia; and the rest by my predecessors for like adequate reasons no doubt. Out of the twenty-nine trials, nineteen convictions were had, each for some grade of criminal homicide, seven for murder in the first degree. Turning now from our survey of the whole district to inspect the record of the Court, which is held at Seattle for the counties of King and Kitsap, and what do we find the trials lasted for the crimes in the first degree. In the Senate, on the 9th, Mr. Call submitted an amendment to the Pensi- rears resolution providing for needy and disabled survivors of the Indian wars prior to 1845, including the Black Hawk, Creek and Seminole wars.

The editorial sanctum of the National Republican, Washington, D.C., was the scene of a tragedy on the night of the 8th. A. M. Soteldo, a committee clerk and newspaper man who had a grievance, called upon Clarence M. Barton, the managing editor, for redress. Pistols were resorted to, and Soteldo was fatally injured, the editor escaping with two slight wounds.

PITNEY, ex-Custodian of the Treasury Department, has revived interest in the contingent fund investigation by adding to his former testimony. He asked to be recalled, Feb. 9th, and stated that he had been informed that Upton and Lamphere had contradicted his testimony with regard to the employees of the Treasury having done work for Secretary Sherman, for which they were paid out of the contingent fund. He reaffirmed his testimony that they had done such work, and had been paid for it out of that fund, and said he was prepared to prove it, and also to prove that Secretary Sherman and Mrs. Sherman knew that this work was so paid for. Senator Hale sprang to his feet, and with some shout of indignation asked: "How dare you charge that Mrs. Sherman knew this?" Pitney replied: "I have received notes from her asking me to send men to do certain work on different occasions, and I have the notes here now." He then produced certain notes, proved to have been written by Mrs. Sherman, requesting that workmen be sent to the Secretary's residence. Pitney added that he had received notes of the same kind from Secretary Sherman, and also produced them.

The following touching incident was telegraphed from Coalfield, Va., the scene of the recent mine horror, on the 7th: Superintendent Dodds mounted a coal car, and, addressing the walling throng of women and children around him, said: "My poor friends, it grieves me to have to state to you that for the present our search for the bodies of those you knew and loved will have to be abandoned. You know what fire in a coal mine means, and it may take months of watching to subdue it. We will close the pit now." The speaker's voice quivered with emotion. He Tries to Brain Sergeant Scott and Officer Butler With an Ax. But Fails.
Yesterday afternoon Sergeant Scott and Officer Butler boarded a Cheasapeake and Ohio train for Overton station, in search of a negro named Bill Williams, an escaped convict from Eusley's plantation. Williams was arrested over a year ago for the shooting of Monroe Alexander, by Captain O'Haver and Sergeant Kuhnholtz. He was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary. He worked on Eusley's plantation for several months, and finally made his escape. Before doing so, he set fire to a storehouse, which was

TOTALLY BURNED.

For six months the police have been looking for him, and information reaching them that Williams was in the neighborhood of Overton, the two officers, as already indicated, set out to catch him. Arriving at Overton Station, which is about six miles from here, they left the train and walked about three miles to the east until they came to the shanty of a negro named Cousins. Here they expected to find their man. Officer Butler approached the cabin and

TAPPED AT THE DOOR.

"Who's there?" came from within.

"A friend," said Officer Butler.

"You can't get in."

"Let me in."

"No, sir; the owner of the house told me to let nobody come in."

The officers held a short and decisive conversation. "Push in the door," said the sergeant. Officer Butler did as directed. The door yielded, and opened as it did so. Officer Butler saw the gleam of an ax in the air, and a blow directed at him cut the rim of his hat. He raised his pistol and

PULLED THE TRIGGER,

but the cartridge snapped and the negro bounded out and began slashing at Sergeant Scott with his murderous weapon. He cut the officer's pants with his ax, but did not hurt him. Seeing that the man was desperate and determined not to be taken, and the lives of both the officers being in danger, the sergeant coolly took aim at the negro and shot him. The criminal ran some twenty yards, and then, in the popular criminal language of the day, "fell with a dull thud." The officers held a rapid consultation. A Convict Shot.
MEMPHIS, January 15.—Jim Titus, alias Bill Williams, colored, a convict who escaped six months ago, was shot and killed this afternoon by Sergeant Scott, of the police force, while resisting arrest. The killing occurred ten miles north of Memphis.

A receiver has been appointed for the World's Mutual Relief Association of Lebanon, Pennsylvania.

Three boys were instantly killed in Brook lyn, the other evening, by the falling of an unoccupied building, in which they were playing.

Hank Pruett, a Lake Erie & Western switchman, just recently married, was killed, at Lafayette, Indiana, last Friday night, while stepping in to pull a pin.

The bridge of the Chicago & Alton Road over Salt river, at Mexico, Missouri, went down with a freight train Saturday morning. Nobody, fortunately, was hurt.

A negro named White pawned an overcoat in St. Louis, Saturday night, and was arrested soon thereafter for stealing the same. He was locked up and the coat identified.

Eph Song, the young man who had a leg run over by a train the other day, just south of Winchester, Illinois, and whose leg was amputated, died Saturday from the effects of it.

Thomas Dolan, a section hand working on the Indianapolis & St. Louis road, just east of Pana, Illinois, was struck by the cars Saturday and seriously injured. He died soon after.

A Mrs. Diggins, whose relatives are among the ultra-fashionable in San Francisco, has just been discovered in criminal intimacy with her husband's friend, named Chase. A divorce, is pending.

General Logerot seized several notables at Stax as hostages for the payment of the war indemnity exacted by France. He threatens severe measures if the money is not forthcoming by the end of January.

Jim Titus, a colored convict; who escaped from Eusley's farm near Memphis, about six weeks ago, was shot and killed by Police Sergeant James Scott, a couple of days since. His whereabouts were discovered, but he refused to surrender to the officers, who thereupon shot him.

Two failures were chronicled on Saturday in Memphis, Tennessee. One of them was E. Lehman, retail clothier, who failed for $10,000, with assets about $5,000, and the other was Joseph Mulcahy, retail grocer, whose liabilities were $7,000; assets not known.

Three suspicious characters were arrested at Pana, Illinois, a few days since with a lot of shoes in their possession. They were detained by Marshal Rosenberry till Saturday, when officers from Madison county went after them, they having obtained the plunder by breaking into a freight car on the Chicago & Alton Road near Alton.

A man who passed under the name of William Wilcox made the acquaintance a few months ago of a girl named Mary Cregel, who was working at the Franklin House in Memphis, and succeeded in enticing her into a mock marriage. Two or three days since the whole thing was discovered, and the girl is almost crazy. Detectives are looking for Wilcox.

The letter read: "I have sent you the small-pox; go home and die." The letter was immediately burned, and the only clue to the perpetrator was thus destroyed, but the best detectives in the country will be set to work on the case.
Sedalia, Missouri, was a couple of days ago the scene of another tragedy. A number of workmen were engaged in erecting a large center-pole for a stone derrick, to be used in removing stone from railroad cars. The pole is about thirty-five feet long, two feet in diameter, and being green oak was very heavy. The workmen had just got the lower end of it into a deep hole and had the pole standing erect. One of the ropes which held it straight broke in two and let the log fall. It crushed Benjamin Ellis to the earth, and crushed him so bad that he died two hours later. Ellis leaves a wife and five children in destitute circumstances.

A fatal accident occurred Saturday afternoon at 1 o'clock on the Missouri Pacific Railroad, near Rose Hill, the first station west of Kirkwood, Missouri. A stranger, supposed to be a stone mason, had been looking for work on the St. Louis & San Francisco construction, and failing to get suitable employment, determined to return to St. Louis. The train was just passing when he got to Rose Hill. In attempting to get on board one of the cars he fell across the rail. A dozen or fifteen cars passed over him, cutting off both legs close up to the trunk. The sight was a horrible one. One leg was crushed out of all shape. The other was found some sixteen feet distant without a scratch upon it excepting where it had been severed from the man's body. Close by, between the rails, was the trunk. The unknown breathed his last as soon as the train men reached him. He was about 40 years of age, and the only paper found upon his body that might possibly lead to his identification, was a letter addressed to "Dennis O'Conol, Bartoid Valley P. O., St. Louis Co., Mo."

TOPLIFF, an old resident of Alamakee County, Iowa, committed suicide by hanging.

MAJOR HICKS, under sentence of death in the Covington (Ky.) jail, has small-pox.

The death is announced of Caroline Richings-Bernard, prominent in English opera some years ago.

PARTICULARS of the recent tragedy near Washington, Wayne County, Ind., are as follows: David Smith and his wife lived in constant warfare for years, in which the boys sided with the mother. She had forced him to sign a deed to the farm and taken the management of it herself. Then she refused to sustain the relation of wife to him any longer. He entered suit to compel her to give back the farm, but compromised by taking half, she agreeing to allow him to occupy the same room with her thereafter. She kept her agreement a few days and then hit him with a boot-jack for kissing her. This was supplemented by a severe thrashing, by the sons. Recently quarreling was renewed in consequence of the sale of a horse, by Daniel, the second son, and Mr. Smith disappeared. Knowing that the boys had threatened the old man's life, neighbors searched for the body and found it in a well, under nineteen feet of water and a pile of stones. There were two holes in the right temple, part of his clothes were torn off, and there were other marks of a scuffle. Investigation led to the discovery that he had been shot by Dan while sitting beside the kitchen fire, and the elder son helped to drag the body out to the barn lot and throw it in the well, while his wife stood guard and kept the smaller children locked up in a bedroom. There was the usual Wednesday reception yesterday, though with less than the usual formality, at the residence of the Secretary of State. Shot and Killed in Prison.

BALTIMORE, March 1.—This afternoon Robert Taylor, a colored convict in the Maryland penitentiary, was shot and killed by Prison Officer James Byrne. Taylor was employed in the foundry and was told by the foreman to go on another floor and make a casting in place of one he destroyed yesterday. He paid no attention to the foreman, when Byrne repeated the order. Taylor replied that he would not go on the other floor, and made an assault on Byrne, when the latter fired. Taylor grappled with the officer, and Mr. Thorne, the foreman, separated them. Taylor than ran for Thorne, but the latter escaped, and he returned to the assault upon Byrne, who fired two more shots, at the last of which Taylor fell and died within an hour. A jury of inquest rendered a verdict that the killing was in self-defense. Taylor was a powerful man, and at times very hard to manage.

A Murderous Convict Shot Down.

The Attempted Assassination of Queen Victoria.
ARREST OF THE MAN WHO FIRED THE SHOT—ATTEMPTS
A cablegram in yesterday's Star announced the firing upon Queen Victoria last evening. A later dispatch from London gave the following particulars: As the Queen was entering her carriage this evening a man in the station-yard deliberately fired a pistol at her. The man, who was a miserable looking object, was immediately seized by several policemen and taken to the Windsor police station. No one was hurt. The man gave his name as Roderick MacLean. The Queen drove off to the castle immediately after she was fired at. The miscreant was followed to the police station by a large crowd of people. The prisoner was with difficulty rescued from the crowd. The Queen arrived at Windsor at 5:25 p.m. She had been in London since Tuesday, where she gave a drawing-room on Wednesday in honor of the Princess Helena, of Waldeck, who is to marry Prince Leopold. A crowd of people assembled at Buckingham Palace this morning in hopes that the Queen would drive out. The demeanor of the people was as cordial as usual. Newspaper hawkers are now (7:30 p.m.) crying the news on the London streets. It causes much sensation.

"There was a large crowd of spectators awaiting the Queen's arrival at Windsor. The Queen walked across the platform of the railway station to her carriage, which was waiting to take her to the castle. John Brown, her attendant, had already ascended to his seat behind the carriage, when a man standing at the entrance to the station-yard, among a number of spectators, pointed a pistol at the carriage and fired. To judge from the report the pistol was not heavily loaded. The Queen, who was probably not aware of what had happened, was immediately driven to the castle, but before she passed the man had been seized by the superintendent of the borough police, who was standing near by. He was also violently seized by the crowd, and was only rescued from them when three or four policemen came to the superintendent's assistance. The pistol was captured by one of the crowd. The prisoner, Roderick MacLean, who was miserably clad, was taken into High street and thence conveyed to the police station in a cab. As soon as the Queen arrived at the castle she ordered an equerry to proceed to the depot to enquire if any one had been hurt. The report of the pistol was sharp, but not loud. MacLean apparently intended firing again, when the revolver, which seemed to be a new one, was knocked from his hand by a bystander and handed to the police. Eton scholars were prominent in the attempt to lynch MacLean. The Right Hon. Sir Henry F. Ponsonby, the Queen's secretary, proceeded to the police station, and after obtaining all the information possible, telegraphed to Mr. Gladstone the facts of the assault. It is understood the Queen has not sustained any shock. MacLean is said to be an inhabitant of the South Sea and is twenty-seven years old. He states that he is a grocer's assistant. The doctors pronounce him sane. The revolver is a six-chambered Colt's, American make. Two chambers were found loaded, and two had recently been discharged. Fourteen ball-cartridges were found on the prisoner. MacLean says that hunger actuated the crime."

Robert Taylor (colored), a convict in the Maryland penitentiary, was shot and killed about 2 o'clock Wednesday afternoon in the foundry at the penitentiary by James Byrne, an officer of the institution. It appears that Taylor, the deceased, had imperfectly done some work the day previous, for which he had been reported by the foreman of the foundry, George W. Thorn, to Officer Byrne, who, under the regulations, sent Taylor to the office of Warden Wilkinson, where he (Taylor) was reprimanded, and told by the warden that he should do the work over after he had finished his task the following day (Wednesday). Accordingly, Wednesday about 1:45 P. M., Mr. Thorn, foreman of the foundry, ordered Taylor, as he had finished his task for the day, to make over the work which he had spoiled the day before. Taylor did not move, and deigned no reply to repeated orders to do the work. Thorn then reported the matter to Officer Byrne, who was in the foundry. That officer ordered Taylor to do the work as instructed by the foreman. Taylor still remained silent, and made no move to obey. Officer Byrne then told Taylor to "go into the office." Taylor said something about getting into trouble, and presently seized a molder's rammer and struck at the officer, who, simultaneously with the demonstration made by Taylor, drew his pistol. As the rammer (a hickory rod one and one-quarter inches in diameter, four feet long, with heavy iron mountings on both ends) descended, the officer threw up his right arm, pistol in hand, received the blow, discharging his pistol, which fell from his hand. The foreman (Thorn) ran up and seized Taylor from behind for a moment or two. Taylor freed himself from Thorn, whereupon Thorn retreated a few steps. Two other shots were fired by Officer Byrne, whose pistol had been returned to him by a convict who was present. Taylor, the colored convict, fell mortally wounded.

The Brutal Treatment Inflicted Upon a Little Girl in an Illinois Town.

STERLING, Ill., Jan. 31. — It has been discovered that a man and woman named Seymour have been horribly maltreating a fatherless girl, seven years old, whom they were supposed to be taking care of. The child is small for its age, and Seymour compelled her to feed and take care of a horse and bring coal. He confined her in a cellar at times all day without food or clothing, except a thin dress, and punished her with a horsewhip until the surface of her entire body was black and blue and sore. Sometimes he would toss her to the ceiling and let her fall on the floor. No species of cruelty seemed too severe to adopt toward the child. The villagers last night made a determined though unsuccessful attempt to lynch Seymour, but both he and his wife have fled.

Anxious to Lynch a Brute.

The village of Rock Falls, Whiteside county, Ill., was in a ferment on Monday. There lives in the place a Mrs Bolton, whose husband has been sent to the insane asylum, leaving her burdened with eight small children. A Times special thus tells the story:

About a month ago one of the children, a girl 7 years old, went to live with a man and woman named Seymour, and Saturday word reached the mother that her child was being abused. She went to Seymour's to inquire into the matter, and found the child in a horrible state from beating and starvation. The child was taken away, put under a physician's care, and warrants issued for the arrest of the guilty parties. Yesterday a great number of people visited the child, and the examination so maddened them that last night about 10 o'clock from twenty to thirty disguised men went to Seymour's house to lynch him. Word came to the man and his wife and they fled. The residence was searched and a number of other houses examined, but he was not caught. Returned Califormans said it looked like old times, and meant business. The child is small for its age, and Seymour compelled her to feed and take care of a horse and bring in coal. He confined her in the cellar at times all day without food or clothing except a thin dress, punished her with a horse-whip until the surface of the entire body was black and blue and sore, and would toss her toward the ceiling and let her fall on the floor. He prevented her going out doors more than once a day, and then when her clothes were soiled compelled her to clean them with her tongue. He insisted upon the child standing on one foot and then when the would become exhausted whipped her with a horsewhip. No species of cruelty seemed too severe to adopt toward the child. The people of the village are determined to have the fellow puished, and will leave no means tried that will reach that result.
